note: Two of the envious, sitting with their eyelids sewn shut. They name themselves later: Guido del Duca, who does nearly all the talking, and Rinieri da Calboli. Both were noblemen of Romagna, the region east of Tuscany.
They cannot see him. They have overheard Dante tell Sapia, in Canto 13, that he is alive and that his eyes are not sewn.
Charity, the love of others, is the virtue the envious are here to learn. The speaker asks for it and shows it in the same breath.
Monte Falterona, in the Apennines east of Florence, where the Arno rises.
The Arno winds for about 150 miles from its source to the sea near Pisa.

context: Dante will not name his city or its river. The rest of the canto gives the reason: in his eyes the whole valley has gone to the bad.

note: Fresh from the terrace of pride, Dante is modest. It is also true for 1300, the year of the journey: he was known in Florence as a love poet, and the Comedy was not yet written.

Not the Alps but the Apennines, the mountain chain that runs the length of Italy. Dante's Italian says only "the rugged mountain". The lines mean that the range is at its most massive around the Arno's source, higher there than almost anywhere else along it.

The cape at the northeast tip of Sicily, facing the toe of Italy. The ancients held that Sicily was once joined to the mainland and that the sea broke it off, so Peloro is the cut end of the Apennines. Virgil tells this in the Aeneid.

quote: what heaven draws up from the sea
note: The water cycle, as Dante's science understood it: the sun lifts water from the sea as vapor, it falls as rain and feeds the rivers, and the rivers carry it back. The phrase means the river's mouth.

context: The people of the Arno valley have turned into beasts, as if by her magic. Guido now follows the river downstream, giving each town its animal.

note: The people of the Casentino, the high valley where the Arno begins. Many readers see a pun on Porciano, a castle there belonging to the Guidi counts: the name sounds like the Italian for pig.
The people of Arezzo: small dogs, all bark.
The Arno flows south toward Arezzo, then a few miles short of the city swings sharply away to the northwest, toward Florence. Dante makes the river do it out of disgust.
The Florentines. The wolf is the poem's animal of greed, like the she-wolf of Inferno 1.
The Pisans, near the river's mouth, who had a name for cunning.
Probably Dante, the Tuscan who will carry the warning home. Some readers take it as Rinieri, who is about to hear his own family shamed.
Guido speaks as a prophet: what follows is revealed to him. For Dante the writer it had already happened, three years after the date of the journey.

Fulcieri da Calboli, Rinieri's nephew. As chief magistrate of Florence in 1303 he served the Black Guelphs, the party that had exiled Dante. He had White Guelphs and Ghibellines arrested, tortured and put to death.
He handed his prisoners over to their enemies for his own gain, like a butcher selling beasts still on the hoof.
Florence. The image recalls the dark forest of the poem's first lines.
Rinieri, hearing what his nephew will do.

quote: what you won't do for me
note: Dante held back his own name, and now asks for theirs.
"Whatever a man sows, that he will also reap" (Galatians 6:7). He sowed envy and harvests stubble: the sewn eyes.

quote: things that must exclude all partnership
note: Worldly goods, such as money, land and rank, where one person's share is another's loss. That is why they breed envy. Dante does not follow, and asks Virgil to explain the phrase in Canto 15.

quote: between the Po, the mountains, sea, and Reno
note: The borders of Romagna: the river Po to the north, the Apennines to the south, the Adriatic Sea to the east, and the river Reno, which flows past Bologna, to the west.

Lizio da Valbona, a Guelph nobleman of the hills above Forlì, who fought alongside Rinieri. Guido now calls a roll of the generous, courteous Romagnoles of the generations before 1300. Several are little more than names today.
A nobleman of Bertinoro, Guido del Duca's own town, and by tradition his close friend.
The great Ghibelline lord of Ravenna, who died in 1225. Guido del Duca was one of his followers.
One of the counts of Carpegna, in the hills of Montefeltro. The early commentators remember him for his open-handedness.

context: Guido has finished with Tuscany and turns on his own region. The sons, he says, are nothing like their fathers.

note: Fabbro de' Lambertazzi, leader of the Ghibellines of Bologna, who died in 1259.
A man of Faenza, born to a family of small farmers, who rose by his own merit to be honored among the nobles. Nobility for Dante is a matter of character, not birth.
From Prata, a village between Faenza and Ravenna. Little else is known of him.
Probably one of the Ubaldini, a Tuscan family with lands in Romagna. That would explain "who lived among us": a Tuscan who made his home there.
A nobleman of the Rimini area, remembered by the early commentators for his hospitality.

quote: the house of Traversara and the Anastagi
note: Two great families of Ravenna. By 1300 both had died out in the male line.

quote: The ladies and knights, the struggles and leisure
note: A famous line, in praise of the lost world of the courts. Two centuries later Ariosto echoed it in the opening line of his Orlando Furioso.
Bertinoro, a hill town between Forlì and Cesena, famous for the hospitality of its noble families. It was Guido del Duca's home.
Bagnacavallo, a town west of Ravenna. Its counts had no sons, and the line was about to end.

quote: Castrocaro does badly, and Conio worse
note: Two castles in Romagna, the first near Forlì, the second near Imola. Their counts were still fathering heirs, and Guido thinks the world would be better without them.

The Pagani were lords of Faenza and Imola. Their "devil" is Maghinardo Pagani, nicknamed the Demon, a cunning warlord who changed sides between Guelphs and Ghibellines as it suited him. He died in 1302. Inferno 27 mentions him too.
A respected nobleman of Faenza who died in 1278. His sons left no heirs, so the family ended before it could decline.
The two souls can hear which way the travelers go. Had it been the wrong way, they would have called out.

quote: Everyone who finds me will kill me!
context: The first example of envy punished, in Cain's own words to God after the murder (Genesis 4:14). Like the examples of love in Canto 13, these come as voices in the air, now loud as thunder.

note: A princess of Athens in Ovid's Metamorphoses. The god Mercury loved her sister Herse. Eaten up with envy, Aglauros sat down in the doorway to keep him out, and he turned her to stone.
The examples of the sin punished, which rein the soul in. Virgil promised in Canto 13 that Dante would hear them before leaving this terrace.
The devil as a fisherman. His bait is the goods of this world.

The heavens, which in Dante's astronomy are great spheres turning around the earth, carrying the sun, the planets and the stars. Their beauty should draw the eyes upward, toward God. The envious kept theirs on their neighbors' goods.
